podcast.title: Supergroup Lineup and Origins (1994-2001)
podcast.body: Tapeworm was conceived as a side project during Nine Inch Nails' "The Downward Spiral" sessions in 1994, intended as a collaborative effort for Danny Lohner and Charlie Clouser. It evolved to include a star-studded lineup: Trent Reznor, Maynard James Keenan (Tool), producer Alan Molder, Atticus Ross, Phil Anselmo and Rex Brown (Pantera), Page Hamilton (Helmet), Toni Halliday (Curve), Tommy Victor (Ministry), and drummer Josh Freese, with at least an album's worth of material recorded by 2001. "If you're Trent Rezner, Danny Loaner and Charlie Closer from his live band, Maynard James Keenan from Tool, producer Alan Molder and Atticus Ross. I mean, wow, awesome, right? The idea for tapeworm went as far back as the sessions for the downward spiral in 1994. Tapeworm was designed as something to which Danny and Charlie could contribute as equals. This idea evolved into something pretty cool. Maynard was brought in, Phil and Salmo from Pantera, Paige Hamilton from Helmut, Tony Haliday from a cool band called Curve, Tommy Victor from Ministry, drummer Josh Freeze. And then in 2001, Alan Molder apparently helped record at least an album's worth of stuff."

podcast.title: Project History (1995-2004)
podcast.body: Tapeworm was a Nine Inch Nails-related side project that existed in various forms from 1995 to sometime in 2004, featuring Trent Reznor and his live band members Danny Loner and Charlie Clouzer. Numerous other artists, including Maynard James Keenan (Tool), producer Alan Molder, Atticus Ross, Paige Hamilton (Helmet), Tony Halliday (Curve), Phil Anselmo (Pantera), and Tommy Victor (Prong, Ministry), were involved. Despite promises of release dates and reports in 2003 that the album was ready to be mixed, the project was ultimately killed by Reznor due to creative differences, Maynard's obligations with A Perfect Circle, and Reznor's decision to resurrect Nine Inch Nails, stating the material "just wasn't good enough." "This was a 9-inch nails-related side project that existed in various forms from 1995 to sometime in 2004... Trent decided to resurrect 9-inch nails. Maynard had obligations with his side projects a perfect circle. There were fights over creative direction, and then Trent killed everything, saying that the material just wasn't good enough."

podcast.title: Project History (1995-2004)
podcast.body: This project was created in 1995 and involved Trent Reznor, Atticus Ross, and a variety of friends, continuing off and on for nine years. Despite the collaboration, nothing was ever officially released. "I already mentioned the tapeworm project, which was created in 1995 and included a lot of different friends. They were continued off and on for nine years, but nothing was ever released."

podcast.title: Recording Sessions and Near Completion (2001-2003)
podcast.body: The Tapeworm project saw significant recording activity, with producer Alan Molder assisting in recording at least an album's worth of material by 2001. Further sessions were held in New Orleans and Atlanta in 2003, with reports indicating that an album was ready to be mixed, suggesting it was close to completion before various obstacles arose. "And then in 2001, Alan Molder apparently helped record at least an album's worth of stuff. In 2003, there were more recording sessions of both New Orleans and Atlanta. And then when we were told that an album was ready to mix."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Survival of Tracks as "Tapeworm DNA"
podcast.body: Despite the Tapeworm album never being officially released, two tracks are noted to carry its "DNA": "Passive" on A Perfect Circle's 2004 album "Emotive" (a descendant of a song called "Vacant"), and "Potions" which appeared on a Puscifer album. These releases offer glimpses into the material created during the project. "Two release tracks do have tapeworm DNA, though. One is called passive. It's on a perfect circle's 2004 album, Emotive. It's a descendant from a song called Vacant. Another is Potions, which appeared on a pusifer album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tapeworm Project Conception (1994)
xref.body: The idea for Tapeworm, a side project intended to allow Danny Lohner and Charlie Clouser to contribute equally, originated during the recording sessions for Nine Inch Nails' 1994 album "The Downward Spiral." This project was envisioned as a collaborative outlet distinct from Trent Reznor's primary creative control over NIN. "The idea for tapeworm went as far back as the sessions for the downward spiral in 1994. Now that was Trent's project. Tapeworm was designed as something to which Danny and Charlie could contribute as equals."

xref.title: Move to Los Angeles (2000)
xref.body: Moved to Los Angeles in 2000 to work on the Tapeworm project with Trent Reznor. "Then in 2000, Atticus moved to LA to be part of a project with Trent called Tapeworm."

xref.title: Charlie Clouser's Departure (2002)
xref.body: In 2002, Charlie Clouser, a member of Nine Inch Nails and a contributor to the Tapeworm project, left Nine Inch Nails and simultaneously severed his connections to Tapeworm. His departure was one of several factors contributing to the eventual demise of the collaborative album. "In 2002, Charlie Closer left 9 inch nails. He also severed connections to the tapeworm project."

xref.title: Trent Reznor Declares Tapeworm "Dead" (Mid-2004)
xref.body: By mid-2004, Trent Reznor officially declared the Tapeworm project "dead for the foreseeable future," signaling the end of the long-gestating supergroup collaboration. Despite multiple recording sessions and an album reportedly ready for mixing, various factors including label disinterest and member commitments led to its abandonment. "And by the middle of 2004, Trent declared that tapeworm was, quote, dead for the foreseeable future."

xref.title: Collaboration with Zack de la Rocha
xref.body: After Zack de la Rocha left Rage Against the Machine in 2000, he embarked on a collaboration with Trent Reznor, which was rumored to have produced up to 20 tracks. Although the project went well from Reznor's perspective, it was ultimately never released, with Reznor stating it "will never see a light of day," a sentiment echoed by de la Rocha who felt uninspired. "I was doing some other musical projects, none of which kind of panned out. And then the tapeworm thing didn't turn out the way we'd hoped. Worked on Zach's Aote Delroge's record. And that went well, but that's never going to see a lighted Aote thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Lost Albums Mentions
xref.body: Trent Reznor mentioned in an interview that he had been involved in other musical projects that didn't pan out, specifically citing the Tapeworm project, Zach De La Rocha's solo record (which he produced), and 12 Rounds' record (which he produced but couldn't be released due to his label's issues). "I was doing some other musical projects, none of which kind of panned out. The tapeworm thing didn't turn out the way it would be to hoped. Worked on Zach Zayot Delroge's record, and that went well, but that's never going to see the light of the day, I don't think. It produced 12 rounds record, but my label was dying, so he couldn't put it down."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ongoing Collaboration with Trent Reznor
xref.body: The experience with Tapeworm, despite not resulting in a release, must have been positive, as Atticus Ross has worked on every Nine Inch Nails album since "With Teeth" (2005). "Atticus has worked on every 9-H nails album since with Teeth in 2005."

xref.title: Record Label Disinterest in Tapeworm
xref.body: The record labels for both Nine Inch Nails and Maynard James Keenan were reportedly "not keen" on the Tapeworm project. This lack of label support, along with scheduling conflicts and internal band dynamics, ultimately prevented the album from being released, despite recording sessions in New Orleans and Atlanta in 2003. "But then reality set in. 9 inch nails record label and Maynard's labels weren't keen on the idea."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Trent Reznor's Rehab and Recovery
xref.body: After the Tapeworm project faced challenges, Trent Reznor entered rehab. Upon his recovery, he expressed a desire to refocus on Nine Inch Nails, a decision that further impacted the viability and completion of the Tapeworm album, especially given Maynard James Keenan's commitments to other bands. "Meanwhile, Trent went into rehab. And when he recovered, he wanted to get back into 9 inch nails."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Unreleased Projects (Tapeworm, Zach de la Rocha solo album)
xref.body: Trent Reznor has several unreleased projects. The Tapeworm project, formed in 1995 with various collaborators, continued off and on for nine years but never released anything. He also produced around 20 tracks for Zach de la Rocha's solo album after Zach left Rage Against the Machine, which Trent considered "excellent," but Zach felt uncomfortable with the results, and it was never released. "I mean, the tapeworm thing didn't turn out the way it would be to hoped. Worked on Zach's, the deal roaches record, and that went well, but that's never going to see the light of day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
